Hi,

So I am working on survey gathered in different centres. So far we have trying to use meta-analysis to combine resutls across centres, or alternatively multi-level models (lmer). However as we only have 3 different centres I would prefer to implement a Bayesian solution and I'm interested to use INLA to do this. There are a couple of things that are unclear to me however. Here is a toy example:

library(INLA)
library(MASS)
dat1 <- birthwt

form1 = low ~ 1 + age + factor(smoke) + f(race, model="iid", hyper=pcprior)
r = inla(form1, family = "binomial", data = dat1, verbose=FALSE)
r$summary.fixed
r$summary.random

So this is typical of the kind of analysis we would like to do. What I'm not clear on is which is the correct model to use - is iid correct for this ? Or rw2? (also I have not yet considered the priors)
I am also wondering about missing predictor data. In the example if some values of age or smoke are missing can INLA cope with that ? So far we have been doing a complete case analysis, alongside an imputed missings analysis (imputation using the mice package).
In the case that I can't deal with missings within INLA, would it be incorrect to apply the inla model on the imputed data ?

Finally - this model allows only an overall effect for smoking - how can I modify it to allow a different effect of smoking per race (or in my real data per centre)

Many thanks,
James

Dear Group,

I ran a zero-inflated negative binomial regression using the multiple likelihood facility. Please see my code with the attached simulated data.

cruise2 <- read.csv(file="cruise_tr1.csv",head=T)

z <- cruise2$count>0 +0
y <- ifelse(cruise2$count>0,cruise2$count,NA)
stk.z <- inla.stack(tag='est.z',
                    data=list(Y=cbind(z,NA)),
                    A=list(1),
                    effects=list(list(z.b0=rep(1,length(z)),
                                      DEPTH.z=cruise2$DEPTH,
                                      dist.z=cruise2$dist)))
stk.y <- inla.stack(tag='est.y',
                    data=list(Y=cbind(NA,y)),
                    A=list(1),
                    effects=list(list(y.b0=rep(1,length(y)),
                                      DEPTH.y=cruise2$DEPTH,
                                      dist.y=cruise2$dist)))
stk.zy <- inla.stack(stk.z,stk.y)
formula2 <- Y ~ 0+z.b0+ DEPTH.z +  dist.z  + y.b0 + DEPTH.y +  dist.y
result.zinb <- inla(formula2,family=c("binomial","nbinomial"),
                    data=inla.stack.data(stk.zy),
                    control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.zy),quantiles=NULL),
                    control.compute=list(dic=TRUE),verbose=TRUE,
                    control.fixed = list(expand.factor.strategy='inla'))
summary(result.zinb)

But I can not figure out a way to generate prediction from the model,

fit <- result.zinb$summary.fitted.values[,"mean"]
lpred <-  result.zinb$summary.linear.predictor[,"mean"]
dim(lpred) <- c(length(y),4)
dim(fit) <- c(length(y),4)
summary(fit[,1]-binomial()$linkinv(lpred[,1]))

The first column of summary.fitted.values seems to be the probability of binomial distribution, but is it possible to calculate predictive values from the model?

Regards
dong

Hi,

i am trying to use INLA to build a Gaussian Process approximation of a complex spatial computer model. The model takes as inputs a vector of parameter, theta, and some spatial (known) inputs X, and provides as an output a map with some predictions.
I have selected random locations in the map, and now I want to approximate the output of my model using a Gaussian Process where the mean depends linearly on theta and X, taking into account the spatial structure of my outputs.

Here is what my data looks like :

0.3054741 4.18219 6.408204   16.71136 1.744384 1.76110  63 159   1 171 159 0.0000000 0.000000e+00  0.19 0.11

for a given run of my computer model, I have the same value for theta (first 5 columns), but I have different locations (x and y) and different values for the spatial inputs (last 4 columns). However, when I run the model with different values for the parameters theta, I am always saving the outputs at the same locations. So in the end, if I run n parameter sets theta_1, ..., theta_n, and save m location points s_1, ..., s_m, I will have n observations at each locations s_1, ..., s_m.

Here is what my code looks like :

locations <- as.matrix(d[,c("x","y")])
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = locations, max.edge = c(20,50), cutoff = 1)

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh)

                    A = list(A,1),

                                   list(b0=d$tau, b1=d$u, b2=d$upsilon, b3=d$propOSR, b4=d$propSNH, b5=d$fc)),

res <- inla(formula,
            data = inla.stack.data(stack),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE))

gproj = inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim=minx:maxx, ylim=miny:maxy)
g.mean = inla.mesh.project(gproj, res$summary.random$field$mean)
g.sd <http://g.sd> = inla.mesh.project(gproj, res$summary.random$field$sd)

I suspect this might arise because I have several observations at the same locations, and so there is a dimension issue. But I havent't been able to solve the problem.

If anyone has an idea or has already done something similar, I would higly appreciate your help!
Thanks
Charlotte

If the option adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE (default) then the model is
adjusted if the graph has more than one connected compoment. This
adjustment can be disabled setting this option to FALSE. If
adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE then constr=TRUE is interpreted as a sum-to-
zero constraint on EACH connected component in the graph and the
rankdef parameter is set to the number of connected components.

see inla.doc("besag")

Best
H

Regarding the marginal likelihood output of the LGCP model using inla (i.e., the "mlik" component of INLA output), I have a few questions:

(1) Is the "mlik" based on the normalized marginal likelihood of the point process?

(2) Refer equation (3)-(4) of Simpson et al. "Going off grid: LGCP" paper,

      (2.1) Is the constant C the same in equation (4) and equation (3), C=|Omega|?
      (2.2) Is the constant C included in "mlik" output or not?
      (2.3) If I want to compare pi(y|z) with pi(y). I use the definition LGCP definition (equation (1)) to calculate f(y|z) given a fixed z, and use the "mlik" output of inla as the value of f(y).  Shall I adjust "mlik" using a constant?

Thank you,

Hongxiao

No, the constant C in (4) is not the same as in (3). In (3) it's |\Omega|, but in (4) it's a combination of \exp(|\Omega|) and the bits of Poisson-probability factors not included in the product. So in conclusion, I believe you're ok as long as you only look at log likelihood differences for a common domain and common data, but would strongly advise agains assuming that this is the case until you and we have verified this by double checking the implementation details.

  https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pscl/vignettes/countreg.pdf
has this to say about quasi-Poisson:
"Another way of dealing with over-dispersion is to use the mean regression function and the variance function from the Poisson GLM but to leave the dispersion parameter φ unrestricted. Thus, φ is not assumed to be fixed at 1 but is estimated from the data. This strategy leads to the same coefficient estimates as the standard Poisson model but inference is adjusted for over-dispersion. Consequently, both models (quasi-Poisson and sandwich-adjusted Poisson) adopt the estimating function view of the Poisson model and do not correspond to models with fully specified likelihoods."

> what would the expression for that likelihood be in that case?

Thanks for your reply,

Let S={y_1, y_2, ...} be a countable set of non-negative numbers (not necessary integers) such that y_i \to \infty as i \to \infty. Then for any \lambda > 0,
   C exp( -\lambda + y_i \log\lambda ) / \Gamma(1 + y_i),   i=1,2, ...
defines a distribution (probability mass function) on S, where
  C = exp(-\lambda) \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}  \exp( y_i \log\lambda ) / \Gamma(1 + y_i) < \infty
is the normalizing factor. Thus the likelihood is proportional to the likelihood of an ordinary Poisson distribution.
This means that the same inference is obtained by using the Poisson likelihood for such data.

In the glm function, family=poisson with non-integer response returns warnings because of calling the Poisson density (mass) function with non-integer values.
> x <- c(2.1, 1.3, 6.2, 7.8, 2.2, 4.6, 3.4, 0.5)
> y <- c(1.4, 1.2, 3.1, 3.2, 1.5, 2.4, 1.8, 0.1)
> glm(y ~ x, family=poisson)

8: In dpois(y, mu, log = TRUE) : non-integer x = 0.100000

But with family=quasipoisson, the same results are obtained with no warnings.

> glm(y ~ x, family=quasipoisson)

So, I guess it depends on the way the Poisson likelihood is implemented in INLA. It seams to work fine.

How does INLA treat non-integer values in the Poisson likelihood?
Does it simply calculate the likelihood at the data points regardless of their type (integer or non-integer)?
